+400 GW project pipeline, up 23 GW or 6% M/M in August. 10 GW got reclassified from hyperscaler to developer; barring this, hyperscalers’ pipeline grew by 6.5 GW, with 6 GW from Amazon. Other large adds were Fermi (10.5 GW), Galaxy (4 GW) and TECfusions (3 GW). On a rolling TTM basis however, pipeline additions stalled at 246 GW. From a geographic standpoint, Texas saw the greatest additions to its pipeline (14.5 GW). Notably, the US is now up to 3 statewide moratoria/pauses (TX, NY, and PA; OH on the way?) which cumulatively represent 40% of the US pipeline. How much is credible? Based on construction stage, tenant credibility, developer characteristics, and regulatory movement, we view 35% or 170GW of the project pipeline as likely to eventually be built. Hyperscaler self-builds dominate with 79% credibility for a total of 73GW. Colocation providers are also high with 67% credibility and 55GW. Neoclouds and miner pivots are at 30% and 23%, respectively (6GW each), with the longtail at 11% (30GW).
Under Construction. Construction grew by 4 GW (up 6% M/M) with Amazon contributing 2 GW; they’re now the first operator to surpass 10 GW of capacity under construction. Colos were largely responsible for the remaining 2 GW with QTS (~750 MW) and STACK (~450 MW) leading the way. On a TTM basis, capacity under construction is down vs. last month, but only by 2%. New construction was largest in Texas (1.9 GW). At today’s build rate, it would take 13 years to clear the 404 GW pipeline, up from 12 years last month.
Stranded Capacity. The rise in local data center opposition ahead of Midterms is starting to have an impact. Stranded capacity grew 7 GW last month, more than the 4 GW added to construction (2nd time in the last 3 months this has happened). On a TTM basis, the pipeline remained flat, construction was down, and stranded capacity was up 13% (Exhibit 7). Moreover, voter opposition continues worsening: 61% of Americans now strongly oppose construction (up from 55% in May), and there are now 25 states restricting or considering restrictions on new construction (up from 18 last month). This may gain even more steam into mid-terms - 70% of capacity in the pipeline and under construction sits in states with upcoming gubernatorial mid-terms, which would double the capacity under risk of potential moratoria/construction pauses (Exhibit 68). After August, stranded capacity as a % of the total pipeline ticked higher to 12%, now the highest level on record (Exhibit 10).

August. 15.7 GW of capacity under construction remained flat M/M. Of note, BTM projects accounted for 64% of the additions to July’s pipeline, above the 41% YTD average. That said, BTM projects are becoming a rising proportion of stranded capacity (27%, up from 16% in May). From an operator type perspective, developers are most reliant on BTM (59% of pipeline), followed by neoclouds (51%). Currently, only 6% of data centers use this approach, though 22% of the capacity under construction will use it, and 40% of projects in the pipeline will use it.

CREDIBILITY ANALYSIS - NEW ANALYSIS ADDED THIS MONTH
In June, we published a detailed analysis trying to separate “credible developers from dudes with powerpoints” that implied ~1/3 of the pipeline capacity (from announced to construction) would actually be built. Our normal, full pipeline dataset casts a deliberately wide net across the North American market: operating facilities, canceled projects, land banks, announcements, and projects already under construction, capturing project-level details including provider, location, construction status, estimated power, disclosed tenant, and other available development factors, with status validated monthly through satellite imagery. But for the credibility analysis, we strip out what is already active and what is knowingly dead, then probability-weight the remaining projects rather than treating every press release as a future build. The probability score is project-specific and reflects four things: stage of development, tenant quality, developer credibility, and state-level regulatory risk. Construction progress carries the most weight—a facility with concrete poured is simply more credible than an announced megabuild—while pre-leasing to an IG hyperscaler, a demonstrated ability to secure power and capital, and a track record of actually delivering capacity all improve the odds. For the full methodology, please see our prior note.
Of the 488GW of capacity currently in our August dataset, we anticipate that 35% of the builds are credible based on today's data. Project Stage is the most meaningful haircut —we consider physical construction progress to be a major indicator of credibility. The tenant haircut is the next most pronounced: for a high-quality, IG tenant, certainty goes up; whereas for some of the miners or longtail neoclouds, credibility is lower. The sponsor haircut is also meaningful, though less so than the prior two —this is a fast-moving space, and we do not want to overpenalize new entrants who are showing clear signs of development and tenant signing. Finally, we layer in a haircut for the location of the build - in states like TX, PA, and NY, who have already announced a pumping of the brakes, we have taken that into account. Our view is not that most of those projects will be canceled - they are more likely to be delayed - but it’s possible that some will fall out. This appears as a relatively small haircut in our analysis (it is also the last of the cuts, operationally).
Since June, our data center pipeline capacity estimates were updated to reflect several changes to tenant credit quality, developer/project execution profiles, and state legislation. On the tenant side, scores were revised to capture evolving counterparty risk, including improved support for Anthropic/Fluidstack through Google's backstop, a stronger credit outlook for Cerebras following its IPO, and a modest reduction for Oracle following its July credit downgrade. On the company side, scores were adjusted based on new customer offtake agreements, financing activity, power infrastructure milestones, and regulatory developments. Notable upgrades were driven by major lease announcements, expanded access to capital, and increased visibility into tenant demand, while Vermaland was downgraded following the regulatory rejection of the La Osa Energy Center project. And on the regulatory side, we were already anticipating movement in TX/PA/NY, but we have revised our scoring to take respective governor actions into account.
